## Previously ...

Four lectures of analysis. All of it assumed the data was real.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

- Identify bot traffic, self-referrals and spam in a GA4 property
- Apply exclusions without destroying the record of what you excluded
- Document the judgement calls behind a cleaned dataset

# 1. What Contaminates Marketing Data

## Bots and Crawlers

GA4 filters traffic from the **IAB known-bot list** automatically, and you cannot
turn it off or see what it removed.

. . .

What it misses: anything not on the list. Scrapers, uptime monitors, link
previewers, and the growing population of AI crawlers reading your pages.

. . .

**Signatures worth looking for:**

- Engagement time of zero, on every session
- Exactly one page per session, always the same one
- Arrivals clustered at 03:00 local time
- A single unusual `hostname`, or a browser version nobody uses

## Self-Referrals

Your own domain appearing in the acquisition report as a traffic source.

. . .

**Cause**: something starts a new session mid-visit. The usual culprits are a UTM
parameter on an internal link (Lecture 9 warned you), a payment or booking page on
another domain, or a subdomain GA4 does not know is yours.

. . .

**Fix**: Admin → Data streams → Configure tag settings → **List unwanted
referrals**, and add your own domains.

. . .

Until you do, your acquisition report says your best traffic source is yourself,
and every channel comparison you make is wrong.

## Internal Traffic

You, reloading your own contact page forty times in Lecture 9 to check the tag
fired.

. . .

**This is in every one of your properties, right now**, and on a site with forty
sessions a week it is not a rounding error. It is the majority of your data.

. . .

Admin → Data settings → Data filters → **Internal traffic**, defined by IP
address. Set it to **Active**, not Testing, or it records the rule and filters
nothing.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Your home IP is probably dynamic and campus is shared. This filter is imperfect
by construction, which is exactly why it belongs in the cleaning log rather than
in your assumptions.
:::

## Referral Spam and Ghost Traffic

Some hits never touched your site at all. Spammers send events directly to
measurement IDs they have guessed or scraped, to get their domain to appear in
your reports.

. . .

Blocking referrers is whack-a-mole. **The durable defence is a hostname filter**:
your real traffic always carries your own hostname, and ghost traffic almost
never does.

. . .

Keep only rows where `hostname` is your domain. One rule, and it holds against
spam you have not seen yet.

## Development and Test Events

The `generate_lead` events you fired in Lecture 9 to prove the tag worked are
indistinguishable, in the export, from real enquiries.

. . .

Two defences, in order of preference:

1. **Prevent**: use GA4's DebugView and the `debug_mode` parameter while testing,
   so test hits are separable at source
2. **Exclude**: drop every event before your launch date, and every event
   matching your own test parameters

. . .

**Exclusion by date is the one every one of you will need**, because none of you
did the first one.

# 2. Cleaning Without Lying

## The Cardinal Rule

<!-- Speaker notes: the difference between cleaning and fabrication is the
     audit trail, not the operation. -->

**Never modify the raw export.**

. . .

The raw file is evidence. It is read-only, it keeps the date you pulled it in its
filename, and nothing ever writes to it.

. . .

Every exclusion is a **step in a script** that reads raw and writes clean. If the
clean file is lost, you rerun the script. If somebody questions a number, you show
them the step.

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
The difference between cleaning and fabricating is not the operation. Deleting
rows is both. The difference is whether the reader can see that you did it.
:::

## The Cleaning Log {.smaller}

One table, kept alongside the script, and shipped with the analysis.

| Rule | Rationale | Rows | Applied | By |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `hostname != mysite.ie` | Ghost spam | 412 | 2026-01-14 | Me |
| Sessions before 2025-10-02 | Pre-launch tag testing | 87 | 2026-01-14 | Me |
| IP 10.x.x.x | My own machine | 233 | 2026-01-14 | Me |
| Zero duration, one page | Bot signature | 51 | 2026-01-16 | Me |

. . .

**Rows removed is not optional.** A rule with no count is a claim; a rule with a
count is a fact somebody else can check.

## Reproducible Cleaning

```
data/
  raw/ga4_export_2026-01-14.csv        <- never edited
  clean/sessions_clean.csv             <- output, regenerable
notebooks/
  01_clean.ipynb                       <- raw in, clean out, prose throughout
  02_analyse.ipynb                     <- reads clean only
```

. . .

The cleaning notebook does one job and says why at every step, in the prose cells
you have been writing since Lecture 13.

. . .

**The test: delete `clean/` and rerun. If you cannot get the same file back, you
do not have a pipeline, you have a memory.**

## Judgement Calls Are Not Errors {.smaller}

Two competent analysts, given the same export, will disagree about:

- Whether a 3-second session is a bounce or a bot
- Whether the viral outlier belongs in the average
- Where the launch date really was
- Whether to exclude a whole country or accept the noise

. . .

**None of those disagreements is a mistake.** Analysis is full of defensible
choices, and pretending otherwise is how people end up hiding them.

. . .

What is not acceptable is that the reader cannot tell which choice you made.
**Documented judgement beats undocumented certainty**, which is the sentence this
module opened with in Lecture 1.

# 4. AI and the Audit Trail

## AI This Block: Agentic coding

Where we are on the module's AI spine, introduced in Lecture 12:

> **Agentic coding.** It writes and runs the analysis. You decide what counts as
> clean.

## AI-Written Steps Are Still Your Steps

An agent will happily write you fifteen cleaning rules in four seconds, and most
of them will be reasonable.

. . .

**The log does not care who wrote the rule.** Every exclusion still needs a
rationale in your own words, and a row count you have looked at.

. . .

The specific risk here: an agent's rules are plausible in general and wrong about
**your** site. It does not know that your launch date was late because the Pages
build failed, or that your flatmate's IP is not internal traffic.

## The Extra Column {.smaller}

One more column on the template from section 2, and it is the one an examiner
will look for.

| Rule | Rationale | Rows | Applied | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Exclude `hostname != mysite.ie` | Ghost spam | 412 | 2026-01-14 | Written by me |
| Exclude sessions under 1s | Bot signature | 88 | 2026-01-14 | Agent-suggested, verified |
| Exclude `country = 'Vietnam'` | — | — | — | **Agent-suggested, rejected** |

. . .

The rejected row stays in the log. **A rule you declined is part of the trail**,
and it is often the most interesting line on the page.

## The Rule

An agent may **propose** an exclusion. Only you may **accept** one.

. . .

Acceptance means you can finish this sentence without looking anything up:

> *I removed these rows because ______, and I know it removed ______ rows.*

. . .

**If you cannot, the rule does not go in**, however sensible it looked.

## Exercise {background="#43464B"}

1. Ask an agent to propose cleaning rules for your export
2. Accept the ones you can justify, reject the rest
3. Record the rejected ones and your reason, which is also part of the trail

::: {#timer2 .timer seconds="900"}
:::
